reviews.early-jurassic-epoch: The Early Jurassic turned on two forces: a supercontinent splitting and a volcanic province erupting. As Pangaea rifted into Laurasia and Gondwana, new seaways such as the Viking Corridor and the Central American Seaway opened, the Central Atlantic began to form, and the Andes and the Pacific plate were born. On land, dinosaurs took over, sauropods became the leading plant-eaters, and the first ornithischians and crabs appeared, while the seas filled with ammonites, plesiosaurs and modern sharks. Then, about 183 million years ago, the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions warmed the climate by 4–8 °C, stripped oxygen from the oceans and drove the Toarcian extinction. The Posidonia Shale of Holzmaden preserves that stagnant sea in exquisite detail.

jura-028.title: Plesiosaurs crowd the earliest Jurassic seas
jura-028.text: Even ichthyosaurs, fast fish-shaped marine reptiles, had something to fear. Large plesiosaurs joined sharks and other ichthyosaurs as their predators. A rich radiation of plesiosaurs is known from the Hettangian, which implies the group had already diversified in the Late Triassic. Most in the Hettangian Blue Lias were short-necked rhomaleosaurids. Plesiosaurs also invaded fresh water, and small forms are known from Jurassic China and Australia. By the Toarcian, about 180 million years ago, longer-necked plesiosaurids reached up to 10 meters.

jura-006.title: Conifers reclaim the fernlands of Sichuan
jura-006.text: Ferns were the survivors. Plants with dissected leaves coped better with the end-Triassic crisis and spread across the boundary into the Jurassic. In China's Sichuan Basin, hot, arid fernlands covered the land at the Triassic–Jurassic transition. In the Hettangian and Sinemurian they gave way to cheirolepid conifers, an extinct family known by its Classopollis pollen. These conifers stayed abundant through the whole Jurassic.

jura-018.title: Seafloor life recovers in fits and starts
jura-018.text: In Britain, seafloor life started recovering almost as soon as the extinction ended. The comeback was not smooth. Repeated relapses into anoxia interrupted it, and oxygen loss and nutrient runoff lasted into the Hettangian, perhaps delaying recovery. In Argentina's Neuquén Basin, communities rebuilt from the late early Hettangian and reached a new balance of diversity by the late Hettangian. The carbon cycle settled only in the Sinemurian, when brachiopods and dasycladacean algae rediversified. Tropical reefs, which had collapsed, did not fully recover until much later in the Jurassic.

jura-001.title: Ammonites rebound from near-extinction
jura-001.text: Ammonoids came within a whisker of extinction at the end of the Triassic. Then they exploded into many new forms with complex sutures, the wavy seams between shell chambers: the ammonites proper. Six orders, from Psiloceratina to Ancyloceratina, all appeared during the Jurassic. Their faunas formed about 20 provinces, grouped into a northern Pan-Boreal and a southern Pan-Tethyan realm. Serpenticone ammonites, coiled like snakes, are abundant in Europe's Jurassic rocks.

jura-003.title: The last coelophysoids and massospondylids disappear
jura-003.text: Not every dinosaur line that survived the end-Triassic extinction lasted long. Basal neotheropods such as coelophysoids and dilophosaurs made it into the Early Jurassic but were gone by the Middle Jurassic. Two-legged basal sauropodomorphs such as the massospondylids also died out by the start of the Middle Jurassic.

jura-008.title: Crocodile relatives multiply, and some go to sea
jura-008.text: Among the crocodile line's few survivors, one branch went to sea. Crocodylomorphs radiated rapidly in the Early Jurassic, filling niches different from those of their Triassic relatives. The mostly marine thalattosuchians first appeared then and became a prominent part of marine ecosystems. One of the oldest, a basal teleosauroid from Morocco, dates from the Hettangian–Sinemurian. On land, a protosuchid from Arizona is the earliest known plant-eating crocodylomorph.

jura-009.title: Dinosaurs take over the land
jura-009.text:
When the end-Triassic extinction cleared away their reptile rivals, dinosaurs did not just survive. They surged. In the Early Jurassic they grew rapidly in both diversity and abundance, and land faunas changed hands. Through the Triassic, dinosauromorphs and pseudosuchians, the crocodile line, had shared the land. Now dinosaurs ruled it alone.

From the Early Jurassic on, dinosaurs and pterosaurs were the commonest land reptiles, while lizards and tuatara relatives filled the roles of small reptiles. By the Early Jurassic at the latest, dinosaurs had spread to every continent. Their reign was long. They stayed the dominant land vertebrates through the rest of the Jurassic and the whole Cretaceous, until 66 million years ago.

jura-010.title: The first certain ornithischians appear
jura-010.text: One of the great dinosaur branches finally shows itself plainly in the Early Jurassic. The earliest definitive ornithischians, the 'bird-hipped' dinosaurs, appeared and diversified then. They were small basal forms such as Lesothosaurus, the heterodontosaurids and early thyreophorans, the armored line. From these modest plant-eaters the group would grow into one of the dinosaurs' main branches.

jura-011.title: The Farallon plate dives beneath North America
jura-011.text: As Pangaea broke apart, an ocean plate began sliding under the American West. In the Early Jurassic, the Farallon plate started sinking beneath western North America. Mountains in Nevada and California kept rising as plate motions pushed North America northward.

jura-017.title: Dicroidium makes a last stand in Antarctica
jura-017.text: The seed fern that once ruled Gondwana's forests ended its days in Antarctica. Dicroidium survived there only as a relict into the Early Jurassic. Its relative Lepidopteris, a peltasperm, likewise lingered in Patagonia.

jura-021.title: Modern sharks and the first rays appear
jura-021.text: Every shark and ray alive today traces back to a radiation that began in the Early Jurassic. Neoselachians, the group of all living sharks and rays, spread out from then on. Rays first appear in the Early Jurassic; the oldest confirmed ray, Antiquaobatis, is from the Pliensbachian of Germany. The oldest six-gilled and carpet sharks come from the Pliensbachian and Toarcian of Europe. By the Late Jurassic, neoselachians had largely replaced hybodonts, the Triassic's dominant sharks. Timelines of Earth and of life date the first rays later, to about 165 million years ago.

jura-024.title: Seawater flips from aragonite to calcite
jura-024.text: Seawater itself changed character in the Early Jurassic. The world's oceans shifted from aragonite-sea to calcite-sea chemistry, two states named for the two forms of calcium carbonate. The new chemistry favored dissolving aragonite and precipitating calcite.

jura-025.title: Cimmeria closes the Paleo-Tethys Ocean
jura-025.text: An old ocean disappeared from west to east, like a zip being closed. In the Early Jurassic, Paleo-Tethys ocean floor subducted beneath the Cimmerian plate, sinking under it until the ocean was gone. The closure was part of the Cimmerian orogeny. Around 200 million years ago, the Tethyan Trench formed as the Cimmerian plate itself subducted beneath eastern Laurasia.

jura-029.title: The Viking Corridor links two oceans
jura-029.text: A seaway several hundred kilometers wide opened between the Baltic Shield and Greenland. From the Early Jurassic, this Viking Corridor linked the Boreal Ocean in the north to the proto-Atlantic. Waters and sea life that had been separated could now mix.

jura-005.title: Coccolithophores and dinoflagellates fill the plankton
jura-005.text: The ocean's chemistry was changed by organisms too small to see. Coccolithophores and dinoflagellates, both first seen in the Triassic, radiated in the Early to Middle Jurassic and became prominent phytoplankton. Coccolithophores have been an integral part of marine plankton ever since. The rise of calcareous plankton in the Middle Jurassic altered ocean chemistry. Their chalky remains, piling up on the seafloor, buffered the oceans against large CO2 emissions. Calcareous nannoplankton kept growing more diverse through the Jurassic and Cretaceous.

jura-030.title: Blue Lias layers keep time with Earth's orbit
jura-030.text: Stripe by stripe, the Blue Lias records the wobble of Earth's orbit. Alternating beds of limestone and shale were laid down from the latest Triassic into the early Sinemurian. Their rhythm records short climate swings driven by Milankovitch cycles, regular changes in Earth's orbit. The rocks are rich in fossils, and most of their Hettangian plesiosaurs are rhomaleosaurids.

jura-031.title: The Andes begin to rise
jura-031.text: The mountain building that raised the Andes has been going on for about 200 million years, and it has not stopped. The Andean orogeny began in the Early Jurassic. Subduction-related volcanism has continued along western South America ever since. The first phases actually stretched the crust, bringing rifting, back-arc basins and the emplacement of large batholiths, huge bodies of cooled magma. Early subduction built the La Negra volcanic arc in northern Chile. The Atacama Fault is thought to have formed as the orogeny began.

jura-033.title: Conodonts vanish after more than 300 million years
jura-033.text: Few animal groups last 300 million years. Conodonts, jawless fish whose tooth-like elements are key index fossils, had survived since the Cambrian. By the end of the Triassic only a handful of species remained, their decline perhaps hastened by the mid-Norian marine crisis linked to the Manicouagan impact. They vanished first in the Tethys and eastern Panthalassa. The last survivors lasted into the earliest Hettangian of Hungary and central Panthalassa, and around 200 million years ago they were gone.

jura-034.title: The Navajo sand sea buries western North America
jura-034.text: The cliffs of Zion Canyon are fossil dunes, up to 670 m thick. In the Jurassic the Colorado Plateau grew ever drier until some 388,000 km² of western North America became a vast desert like the Sahara. The Navajo Sandstone formed in this erg, a sand sea, on western Pangaea, swept by winter monsoon winds. A 2019 radioisotopic study puts its start around 200–195 million years ago.

jura-035.title: Pangaea tears into Laurasia and Gondwana
jura-035.text:
The supercontinent that held every major landmass began to come apart around 200 million years ago. By then the Central Pangean Mountains had worn down to a few uplands, and widespread magmatism, including the Karoo and Ferrar provinces, preceded the rupture. The breakup ran to about 160 million years ago.

Through the Early Jurassic, Pangaea split into Laurasia, Eurasia and North America, in the north and Gondwana in the south. By the Middle Jurassic it had fully broken up. The parting opened the Tethys between the landmasses and greatly strengthened the water cycle. Another source has the Tethys Seaway splitting Pangaea in two only in the Late Jurassic, though. North and South America separated in the Late Jurassic. By about 150 million years ago, their divergence was making oceanic crust off Colombia's Pacific coast.

jura-032.title: A seaway opens between the Americas
jura-032.text: When the Jurassic began, North and South America were still joined. By the start of the Late Jurassic they had rifted apart, and a seaway ran between them. The Central American Seaway, also called the Hispanic Corridor, formed between about 200 and 154 million years ago, during the first breakup of Pangaea. It linked the North Atlantic and Tethys with eastern Panthalassa. Fossils suggest it was already open in the Early Jurassic. It closed only when the Isthmus of Panama formed.

jura-038.title: Vulcanodon and the first true sauropods
jura-038.text: Ledumahadi of South Africa already weighed about 12 tonnes, far more than other early sauropodomorphs, and it walked on four legs. Soon after, the true giants' line appeared. Gravisaurian sauropods first appeared in the Early Jurassic, and the oldest definite one, Vulcanodon of Zimbabwe, is likely Sinemurian. By the end of the Early Jurassic, possibly after a global warming event, sauropods had become the dominant large plant-eaters on land.

jura-039.title: Sea level climbs, then falls back
jura-039.text: The early Jurassic sea rose and fell like a slow tide. Through the Hettangian and Sinemurian it stayed near today's level. In the late Sinemurian and Pliensbachian it rose several tens of meters. By the late Pliensbachian it had fallen back to near present levels.

jura-040.title: Saltriovenator, the oldest known ceratosaur
jura-040.text: Italy holds the oldest known ceratosaur. Saltriovenator comes from the early Sinemurian, 199.3–197.5 million years ago. It belongs to the averostrans, an advanced group of theropods whose earliest members appeared in the Early Jurassic.

jura-041.title: A long cool spell chills the Early Jurassic
jura-041.text: Dropstones, rocks carried by ice and dropped into seafloor mud, turn up in northeastern Siberia. With glendonites, crystals that form in cold water, they point to cold winters in the Early to Middle Jurassic. The first part of the Jurassic was a cool interval lasting from about 199 to 183 million years ago. Evidence suggests the late Pliensbachian was an icehouse, perhaps with Northern Hemisphere glaciation early and late in the stage. The cool interval ended with a 4–8 °C warming spike in the early Toarcian.

jura-044.title: Lyme Regis mudstones yield the armored Scelidosaurus
jura-044.text: Complete skeletons of an armored dinosaur come out of the cliffs of Lyme Regis and Charmouth, England. The Charmouth Mudstone yields Scelidosaurus along with plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs. It also holds large numbers of exceptional fish and a diverse insect fauna.

jura-046.title: The Puchezh-Katunki impact scars western Russia
jura-046.text: Buried beneath western Russia lies one of the major impact scars of the Jurassic. Argon–argon dating places the strike, in today's Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, at 195.9 ± 1.0 million years ago, in the Sinemurian. The crater is 40 km across from rim to rim. Including its ring terrace, it spans about 80 km.

jura-049.title: Eocarcinus, the first true crab
jura-049.text: The first true crab did not yet look like a crab. Eocarcinus praecursor, from the early Pliensbachian of England, is the earliest true crab, but it still lacked the body shape of modern crabs. Crabs and shrimp both appear in the Jurassic.

jura-051.title: Volcanoes erupt across southern Sweden
jura-051.text: A volcanic mudflow made a time capsule in Sweden. In central Skåne, volcanism had its first and main phase from the late Sinemurian to the Toarcian, about 191 to 178 million years ago. At Korsaröd a lahar, a flow of volcanic mud, buried Early Jurassic wood, pollen and spores and preserved them exceptionally well.

jura-053.title: The first pliosaurs enter the seas
jura-053.text: About 190 million years ago, pliosaurs, short-necked plesiosaurs, entered the fossil record. They arrived in busy seas. Many groups of primitive sea invertebrates appeared about the same time, and sponge reefs developed extensively.

jura-054.title: The Pacific plate is born as a microplate
jura-054.text: Today's largest tectonic plate began as a small one. Around 190 million years ago, the Pacific plate originated as a microplate where three plates met: the Farallon, Phoenix and Izanagi. A kink in one plate boundary turned this stable triple junction into an unstable one ringed by transform faults. The new plate formed at its center. It was born far from the margins of the Paleo-Pacific Ocean, in central Panthalassa.

jura-055.title: A small impact leaves the Viewfield crater
jura-055.text: Not every impact is a giant. A small one made the Viewfield crater in Saskatchewan, Canada, just 2.5 km across. It struck about 190 ± 20 million years ago, in the Late Triassic or Early Jurassic.

jura-056.title: Dilophosaurus, the double-crested hunter of Arizona
jura-056.text: At about 7 m long and 400 kg, Dilophosaurus was the largest known land animal in North America in its day. This theropod, with a pair of thin arched crests on its skull, lived about 186 million years ago. Known from Arizona's Kayenta Formation, it was one of the earliest large predatory dinosaurs and is cast as a top predator of its time. Eubrontes footprints are widely credited to a theropod like it.

jura-059.title: Eutriconodont mammals make their debut
jura-059.text: When eutriconodonts first show up, in the Toarcian, they already come in several groups, such as Argentoconodon. These early mammals went on to live across Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas during the Jurassic and Cretaceous.

jura-065.title: The Toarcian extinction wipes out most Tethyan corals
jura-065.text: For the corals of the Tethys, it was a catastrophe: 90.9% of species and 49% of genera were wiped out. The Toarcian extinction, about 183 million years ago, struck in two pulses, the Pliensbachian–Toarcian boundary event and the larger pulse of {{ref:jura-071}}. Ammonoids, already squeezed by the Gibbosus Event a million years earlier, suffered further losses. On land, seed ferns and spore plants declined, possibly from mercury poisoning. Later in the Toarcian, megalosaurid dinosaurs diversified, perhaps filling niches the die-off had emptied.

jura-067.title: Karoo-Ferrar lavas flood southern Gondwana
jura-067.text:
About 2.5 million cubic kilometers of magma poured out across southern Africa and Antarctica. The Karoo and Ferrar provinces erupted about 183 million years ago, just before Gondwana's breakup, making one of Earth's most extensive large igneous provinces.

As southern Africa passed over the Bouvet hotspot, basalt flooded the Clarens desert and covered nearly all of southern Africa. Magmatism spread to Namibia, Lesotho, Lebombo and Antarctica by 184–175 million years ago. Patagonia's Chon Aike province peaked 183–173 million years ago. The timing matters. It matches the Toarcian anoxic event and the Pliensbachian–Toarcian extinction, tying these eruptions to one of the Jurassic's great crises.

jura-069.title: Holzmaden's Posidonia Shale preserves skin and blood cells
jura-069.text: An ichthyosaur 182.7 million years old still held collagen and blood cells. It comes from the Posidonia Shale at Holzmaden, Germany, laid down about 183 million years ago during the Toarcian anoxic event. The stagnant, oxygen-free basin preserved superb complete skeletons of fish and marine reptiles, and one plesiosaur kept traces of its skin. Its quality of preservation became a benchmark for other fossil sites.

jura-071.title: Oxygen drains from the Toarcian oceans
jura-071.text:
About 183 million years ago, early in the Toarcian, oxygen vanished from wide areas of the ocean. This Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event is the only one documented from the Jurassic. It was possibly the most extreme case of widespread ocean deoxygenation in the whole Phanerozoic.

The chain began with volcanoes. Carbon dioxide from the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions warmed the climate, acidified the oceans and sped up weathering on land. The flood of nutrients washed into the sea and eutrophied it, overfeeding plankton until the water lost its oxygen. The carbon release was large enough to disrupt the otherwise steady 9-million-year carbon cycle of the Jurassic. The stagnant seas laid down organic-rich black shales, including oil shales now mined commercially in China.

jura-072.title: A Toarcian heat spike pushes seas past 30 °C
jura-072.text: Pangaea's interior probably passed 40 °C, and sea surface temperatures likely topped 30 °C. Early in the Toarcian, global temperatures spiked by about 4–8 °C, and the warm interval lasted until about 174 million years ago. A brief cold snap interrupted the warming just before the anoxic event. The rapid heating intensified tropical storms worldwide, and a stronger water cycle made lakes expand. Sea level rose gradually through the Toarcian to a peak about 75 meters above today's.

jura-075.title: The Central Atlantic begins to open
jura-075.text: Some of the oldest ocean floor still on Earth, about 180–200 million years old, lies in the northwest Atlantic and west Pacific. Its story starts in the Early Jurassic. Rifting between North America and Africa came first, opening rift basins such as the Newark Basin from Mexico to Nova Scotia. About 180 million years ago, the central Atlantic began opening as a narrow ocean between Pangaea's northern and southern parts. Seafloor spreading between North America and Africa–South America began the breakup of Pangaea. The North Atlantic stayed narrow through the Jurassic, and the South Atlantic did not open until the Cretaceous.

jura-076.title: Gondwana starts to come apart
jura-076.text: The southern supercontinent began to break after a burst of lava. Gondwana started fragmenting around 180 million years ago, following the fast emplacement of the Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts. Madagascar and Antarctica began rifting away from Africa, opening the western Indian Ocean. The oldest magnetic anomalies show the first break in today's southern Weddell Sea, about 180 to 160 million years ago. Farther west, rifting at Falkland latitudes began about 190 million years ago, pushing Patagonia westward. The breakup sped up in the Cretaceous and was largely complete by its end.
